title: Bear and Paradox
statementMd:
Limak is a big polar bear. He prepared $*n*$ problems for an algorithmic contest. The $*i*$-th problem has **initial** score $*p*_{*i*}$. Also, testers said that it takes $*t*_{*i*}$ minutes to solve the $*i*$-th problem. Problems aren't necessarily sorted by difficulty and maybe harder problems have smaller initial score but it's too late to change it — Limak has already announced initial scores for problems. Though it's still possible to adjust the speed of losing points, denoted by $*c*$ in this statement.

Let $*T*$ denote the total number of minutes needed to solve all problems (so, $*T* = *t*_{1} + *t*_{2} + ... + *t*_{*n*}$). The contest will last exactly $*T*$ minutes. So it's just enough to solve all problems.

Points given for solving a problem decrease linearly. Solving the $*i*$-th problem after $*x*$ minutes gives exactly ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/c2c3d2323710b5236e42078b445a8cc586f0800e.png) points, where ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/64f50f66d213ce98d5ae4014b8736c50e1aecfe2.png) is some real constant that Limak must choose.

Let's assume that $*c*$ is fixed. During a contest a participant chooses some order in which he or she solves problems. There are $*n*!$ possible orders and each of them gives some total number of points, not necessarily integer. We say that an order is *optimal* if it gives the maximum number of points. In other words, the total number of points given by this order is greater or equal than the number of points given by any other order. It's obvious that there is at least one optimal order. However, there may be more than one optimal order.

Limak assumes that every participant will properly estimate $*t*_{*i*}$ at the very beginning and will choose some optimal order. He also assumes that testers correctly predicted time needed to solve each problem.

For two distinct problems $*i*$ and $*j*$ such that $*p*_{*i*} < *p*_{*j*}$ Limak wouldn't be happy to see a participant with strictly more points for problem $*i*$ than for problem $*j*$. He calls such a situation a *paradox*.

It's not hard to prove that there will be no paradox for $*c* = 0$. The situation may be worse for bigger $*c*$. What is the maximum real value $*c*$ (remember that ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/64f50f66d213ce98d5ae4014b8736c50e1aecfe2.png)) for which there is no paradox possible, that is, there will be no paradox for **any optimal order** of solving problems?

It can be proved that the answer (the maximum $*c*$ as described) always exists.

## Input

The first line contains one integer $*n*$ ($2 ≤ *n* ≤ 150 000$) — the number of problems.

The second line contains $*n*$ integers $*p*_{1}, *p*_{2}, ..., *p*_{*n*}$ ($1 ≤ *p*_{*i*} ≤ 10^{8}$) — initial scores.

The third line contains $*n*$ integers $*t*_{1}, *t*_{2}, ..., *t*_{*n*}$ ($1 ≤ *t*_{*i*} ≤ 10^{8}$) where $*t*_{*i*}$ is the number of minutes needed to solve the $*i*$-th problem.

## Output

Print one real value on a single line — the maximum value of $*c*$ that ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/64f50f66d213ce98d5ae4014b8736c50e1aecfe2.png) and there is no optimal order with a paradox. Your answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed $10^{ - 6}$.

Namely: let's assume that your answer is $*a*$, and the answer of the jury is $*b*$. The checker program will consider your answer correct if ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/fb10c3e3b874552413ba93d1cdf2971c83f2ebe0.png).

## Note

In the first sample, there are $3$ problems. The first is $(4, 1)$ (initial score is $4$ and required time is $1$ minute), the second problem is $(3, 1)$ and the third one is $(10, 8)$. The total time is $*T* = 1 + 1 + 8 = 10$.

Let's show that there is a paradox for $*c* = 0.7$. Solving problems in order $1$, $2$, $3$ turns out to give the best total score, equal to the sum of:

1. solved $1$ minute after the start: ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e300b226dba2622235193889de3334147547cfcb.png)
2. solved $2$ minutes after the start: ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/899352b92886f248a9c8e31247a7e4043f9f45e9.png)
3. solved $10$ minutes after the start: ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/ed13f9d5e6cc1ef056b90a9157397d02abab0b16.png)

So, this order gives $3.72 + 2.58 + 3 = 9.3$ points in total and this is the only optimal order (you can calculate total scores for other $5$ possible orders too see that they are lower). You should check points for problems $1$ and $3$ to see a paradox. There is $4 < 10$ but $3.72 > 3$. It turns out that there is no paradox for $*c* = 0.625$ but there is a paradox for any bigger $*c*$.

In the second sample, all $24$ orders are optimal.

In the third sample, even for $*c* = 1$ there is no paradox.
statementZhMd:
Limak 是一只巨大的北极熊。他为一场算法竞赛准备了 $*n*$ 道题。第 $*i*$ 道题的**初始**分数为 $*p*_{*i*}$。测试人员还表示，解决第 $*i*$ 道题需要 $*t*_{*i*}$ 分钟。题目不一定按照难度排序，较难的题目可能反而有更低的初始分数，但现在已经来不及修改了——Limak 已经公布了各题的初始分数。不过，他仍然可以调整分数下降的速度，在本题中记为 $*c*$。

令 $*T*$ 表示解决所有题目所需的总时间（即 $*T* = *t*_{1} + *t*_{2} + ... + *t*_{*n*}$）。比赛将恰好持续 $*T*$ 分钟，因此时间刚好足够解决所有题目。

解决题目所得的分数会线性下降。在比赛开始 $*x*$ 分钟后解决第 $*i*$ 道题，恰好可以获得 ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/c2c3d2323710b5236e42078b445a8cc586f0800e.png) 分，其中 ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/64f50f66d213ce98d5ae4014b8736c50e1aecfe2.png) 是 Limak 必须选择的某个实数常量。

假设 $*c*$ 已经确定。比赛过程中，参赛者需要选择解决题目的顺序。一共有 $*n*!$ 种可能的顺序，每种顺序都会得到一定的总分，该总分不一定是整数。如果某种顺序得到的总分最大，我们就称其为**最优顺序**。换句话说，该顺序得到的总分大于或等于其他任何顺序得到的总分。显然，至少存在一种最优顺序。不过，最优顺序可能不止一种。

Limak 假设每位参赛者都会在比赛开始时正确估计 $*t*_{*i*}$，并选择某个最优顺序。他还假设测试人员正确预测了解决每道题所需的时间。

对于两个不同的题目 $*i*$ 和 $*j*$，如果 $*p*_{*i*} < *p*_{*j*}$，那么如果参赛者在题目 $*i*$ 上获得的分数严格高于题目 $*j*$，Limak 就会感到不满。他将这种情况称为一个**悖论**。

不难证明，当 $*c* = 0$ 时不会出现悖论。对于更大的 $*c*$，情况可能会变糟。请你求出最大的实数 $*c*$（注意 ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/64f50f66d213ce98d5ae4014b8736c50e1aecfe2.png)），使得不可能出现悖论，即对于**任何最优顺序**，都不会出现悖论。

可以证明，答案（上述意义下的最大 $*c*$）总是存在。

## 输入格式

第一行包含一个整数 $*n*$（$2 ≤ *n* ≤ 150 000$），表示题目的数量。

第二行包含 $*n*$ 个整数 $*p*_{1}, *p*_{2}, ..., *p*_{*n*}$（$1 ≤ *p*_{*i*} ≤ 10^{8}$），表示各题的初始分数。

第三行包含 $*n*$ 个整数 $*t*_{1}, *t*_{2}, ..., *t*_{*n*}$（$1 ≤ *t*_{*i*} ≤ 10^{8}$），其中 $*t*_{*i*}$ 表示解决第 $*i*$ 道题所需的分钟数。

## 输出格式

在一行中输出一个实数，即满足 ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/64f50f66d213ce98d5ae4014b8736c50e1aecfe2.png) 且不存在带有悖论的最优顺序时 $*c*$ 的最大值。如果你的答案与标准答案的绝对误差或相对误差不超过 $10^{ - 6}$，则会被判定为正确。

具体来说，假设你的答案为 $*a*$，标准答案为 $*b*$。如果 ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/fb10c3e3b874552413ba93d1cdf2971c83f2ebe0.png)，则评测程序会认为你的答案正确。

## 说明

在第一个样例中，有 $3$ 道题。第一道题是 $(4, 1)$（初始分数为 $4$，需要 $1$ 分钟解决），第二道题是 $(3, 1)$，第三道题是 $(10, 8)$。总时间为 $*T* = 1 + 1 + 8 = 10$。

下面说明当 $*c* = 0.7$ 时会出现悖论。按照 $1$、$2$、$3$ 的顺序解决题目时，总分最高，等于以下分数之和：

1. 在比赛开始 $1$ 分钟后解决第 $1$ 题：![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e300b226dba2622235193889de3334147547cfcb.png)
2. 在比赛开始 $2$ 分钟后解决第 $2$ 题：![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/899352b92886f248a9c8e31247a7e4043f9f45e9.png)
3. 在比赛开始 $10$ 分钟后解决第 $3$ 题：![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/ed13f9d5e6cc1ef056b90a9157397d02abab0b16.png)

因此，该顺序的总分为 $3.72 + 2.58 + 3 = 9.3$，并且这是唯一的最优顺序（你也可以计算其他 $5$ 种顺序的总分，验证它们都更低）。检查第 $1$ 题和第 $3$ 题所得的分数即可发现悖论：虽然有 $4 < 10$，但 $3.72 > 3$。事实证明，当 $*c* = 0.625$ 时不会出现悖论，而对于任意更大的 $*c*$ 都会出现悖论。

在第二个样例中，全部 $24$ 种顺序都是最优顺序。

在第三个样例中，即使 $*c* = 1$，也不会出现悖论。
